The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{x}^{1/x}y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{1/x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}-x]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}+1-(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{11}{6}) \\  & =\frac{11}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the line
$y=1-x$ and the coordinate axes.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/95ebd0a4eb874972b459e53eecf1d57650f63284698fcad967c09620ac01cd99.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=1-x$ intercepts the $x$-axis at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/d048f20f2299722cee598cc1005237627ecdd7643e996b269f26b5a096f01f2f.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1-x}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dA={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{-x+1}\frac{1}{(1+x+y)^{2}}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{1}{1+x+y}]}_{0}^{-x+1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{1+x+(1-x)}-(-\frac{1}{1+x+0}))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1+x})dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}x+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-(0+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines
$x=e,$ $y=e$ and the curve $y={e}^{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/aa635ca5ef3198fea56d684b034de476a72e4ace2a4c51b37c6c59977036eb76.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=e$ intercepts the curve $y={e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$1\le x\le e.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14114783/assets/b78021a06c9fea100b75c66a619c425345cda3666d84da018895be15a53af06d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,e\le y\le {e}^{x}}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{y\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)]}_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}]_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{4}-{x}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{4})\,dx & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x-\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+1-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{14}{15}\end{aligned}
$$
